# Parse, Don't Validate: Boundaries and Retained Knowledge

## Keep the result of checking

Alexis King's “Parse, don't validate” is not merely advice to check early
[@king2019]. It asks what representation remains after the check. A predicate
can report that a value is acceptable and then discard the reason. A parser
returns a value whose representation records what was established.

King's contrast is usefully concrete. A function with the shape
`validateNonEmpty :: [a] -> ()` inspects a list, fails when it is empty, and
returns no evidence when it succeeds. A later consumer receives the same
`[a]` and must trust a convention or ask the same question again.
`parseNonEmpty :: [a] -> NonEmpty a` performs the same inspection but returns
a representation that retains the result. The important difference is not
whether a check ran; it is whether the program kept what the check learned.

Two common pathologies follow when it does not. **Shotgun parsing** scatters
recognition and rejection across the processing pipeline, so code begins
acting on input before deciding what the input means and may discover a
problem only after side effects or expensive work. **Boolean blindness**
compresses a richer fact into `TRUE` or `FALSE`: the bit records that some
predicate succeeded but carries neither the established structure nor the
reason it matters. Both pathologies force downstream code to reconstruct
knowledge the boundary already possessed.

In R, this is a runtime discipline rather than a compile-time proof:

> A boundary accepts uncertain input and returns a value with a narrower,
> documented meaning, or it reports why no such value can be produced.

An S7 object can therefore act as a **construction certificate**, but only
within a stated boundary. It certifies:

- the property and class invariants visible when it was constructed;
- the aggregate invariants visible to the aggregate root, if construction
  passed through that root;
- continued validity under the update paths the API promises to support.

It does not certify facts that require unavailable context, laws never
encoded, or the future contents of reference-valued payloads. Low-level
mutation, unchecked validation escape hatches, and a mutable environment
stored inside an otherwise valid object can all invalidate stronger claims.
A getter's result also needs its own contract; a declared property class does
not by itself prove arbitrary computed output.

The useful claim is consequently precise: consumers may rely on the
invariants established by the supported construction and transformation
paths. Package authors make that claim credible by keeping those paths small,
documented, and tested.

The progression from a primitive to a domain value makes the claim tangible.
A character string `"#336699"` is only text; a successful `parse_color()`
can return a `Color` whose channels are canonical finite integers in the
declared range. Code that accepts `Color` need not repeatedly parse the hex
spelling or re-check those channel laws. The object acts as a certificate for
exactly those bounded facts. It is not a proof that an arbitrary getter is
correct, that reference-valued internals never changed, or that every target
renderer supports the color. Those stronger claims belong to other
boundaries.

S7's deferred-validation escape hatches make the boundary especially worth
stating precisely. The detailed behavior of `S7::valid_eventually()` and
`S7::valid_implicitly()`, including the difference between final validation
and no final validation, is developed in
[Chapter 2](02-values-and-state.qmd). Here the architectural conclusion is
enough: supported construction and update paths preserve the advertised
certificate; unchecked internal paths transfer the proof obligation to their
caller.

## The same boundary move in several ecosystems

The representation move is broader than any one object system. These small
examples all replace an unchecked number with a named positive budget, but
their guarantees are not identical. Haskell and Rust can make the unchecked
representation unavailable to statically typed consumers; Zod combines a
runtime parser with a TypeScript brand; S7 gives R a nominal runtime value
whose constructor and supported replacement paths enforce the contract
[@ghc-newtype; @rust-tryfrom; @zod-brand].

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R and S7

```r
PositiveBudget <- S7::new_class(
  "PositiveBudget",
  properties = list(value = S7::class_double),
  validator = function(self) {
    value <- self@value
    if (length(value) != 1L || !is.finite(value) || value <= 0) {
      return("`value` must be one finite positive number")
    }
    NULL
  }
)

parse_budget <- function(x) {
  PositiveBudget(value = as.double(x))
}
```

### Haskell

```haskell
newtype PositiveBudget = PositiveBudget Double

mkPositiveBudget :: Double -> Either String PositiveBudget
mkPositiveBudget x
  | isNaN x || isInfinite x || x <= 0 =
      Left "budget must be finite and positive"
  | otherwise = Right (PositiveBudget x)
```

### Rust

```rust
struct PositiveBudget(f64);

impl TryFrom<f64> for PositiveBudget {
    type Error = &'static str;

    fn try_from(value: f64) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        if value.is_finite() && value > 0.0 {
            Ok(Self(value))
        } else {
            Err("budget must be finite and positive")
        }
    }
}
```

### TypeScript and Zod

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const PositiveBudget = z
  .number()
  .finite()
  .positive()
  .brand<"PositiveBudget">();

type PositiveBudget = z.infer<typeof PositiveBudget>;

const parseBudget = (input: unknown): PositiveBudget =>
  PositiveBudget.parse(input);
```

:::

The transferable lesson is not that S7 turns R into one of these languages.
It is that a successful boundary should leave behind a representation that
retains the distinction it just established.

## Three different boundary decisions

Strict construction, tolerant parsing, and compilation answer different
questions.

**Strict construction** creates a known domain value. `RunSpecification()`
may require a bounded positive budget, a supported method, a valid candidate
set, and a coherent relationship between its properties. Failure means no
`RunSpecification` exists.

**Tolerant parsing** admits foreign or versioned input. It need not pretend
that every input is known:

- recognized and complete input becomes a known variant;
- useful but unsupported input becomes an explicit `UnknownSpecification`;
- incomplete input becomes a `PartialSpecification` carrying diagnostics;
- input with no useful recoverable structure causes a condition.

Tolerance preserves knowledge only when uncertainty is represented. Returning
a known class after silently dropping unknown fields is not tolerant parsing;
it is lossy translation.

**Compilation** applies a target policy. A parser may preserve an unknown
variant so that a document can be inspected or round-tripped, while
`compile_run()` rejects it because the execution engine cannot assign it
meaning. Parsing asks what can be represented; compilation asks what this
target can execute.

This separation avoids two bad extremes: making every reader reject future
content, and letting unknown content reach an executor as though it were
understood.

The three decisions can form one continuous pipeline rather than three
competing APIs. A tolerant reader first preserves what it can know. A strict
constructor mints a `RunSpecification` only for a recognized, intrinsically
lawful request. `prepare()` combines that specification with data and target
context to produce `PreparedRun`, and `execute()` accepts only the prepared
form. Unknown or partial parse variants remain inspectable and
round-trippable, but `compile_run()` refuses them unless its target policy
defines a lowering. Each arrow strengthens or preserves knowledge; none
silently claims more than its inputs justify.

## Constructors normalize; validators verify

Boundary functions may accept several input spellings, normalize names,
coerce values under an explicit policy, and attach diagnostics. Constructors
for known classes then receive canonical property values.

Validators should verify those canonical values, not repeatedly parse them.
A property validator handles local laws such as length, range, membership,
or a pattern. It returns `NULL` on success or a character vector containing
one or more problems. A class validator handles relationships among the
properties it can see and likewise may return multiple problems.

That cardinality matters. Reporting several independent violations in one
construction attempt can be useful, and S7 validators are not limited to one
message.

## One authoritative definition, several uses

A rule may be enforced or exposed in several places without having several
independent meanings. A declared bound might drive:

- an S7 validator;
- a JSON Schema projection;
- input-widget limits;
- reference documentation;
- a fast boundary check with a more local error.

The goal is **one authoritative definition**, not one execution. Projections
and duplicated enforcement can drift or contain bugs, so agreement is a test
obligation rather than an automatic guarantee. When a rule cannot be
projected faithfully, name the authoritative form and document the weaker
projection.

This changes how to use a checking ladder. The ladder identifies the smallest
boundary with enough information to state a rule coherently:

1. an external conformance authority for a foreign wire contract;
2. a parser for coercion, version handling, and unknown input;
3. a property class and validator for one canonical property;
4. a class validator for relationships within one object;
5. an aggregate root for references and relationships among contained
   objects;
6. an operation for contextual requirements and legal transitions;
7. an internal assertion for states believed to be impossible.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-checking-ladder
%%| fig-cap: "Place each rule at the first boundary with enough information to state it coherently."
flowchart TB
  Wire["External conformance"] --> Parse["Parsing and normalization"]
  Parse --> Property["Property class and local law"]
  Property --> Entity["Relationships within one object"]
  Entity --> Aggregate["References across an aggregate"]
  Aggregate --> Context["Contextual preparation or transition"]
  Context --> Assertion["Internal assertion"]
```

The ladder in @fig-checking-ladder is about information visibility, not
merely nesting. A child cannot
certify a sibling relationship it cannot see. A root should not absorb a
requirement that also needs a dataset, host policy, database catalog, or
other external authority.

It is also a defense against shotgun parsing. The request enters through one
parser, local laws become properties of `RunSpecification`, aggregate laws
are checked where the complete request is visible, and contextual laws are
resolved by `prepare()`. By the time execution begins, each question has one
named home and a representation records its answer.

## Contextual preparation

Consider a computation request:

```text
loose input
    -> RunSpecification
    -> prepare(specification, dataset)
    -> PreparedRun
    -> execute()
```

`RunSpecification` can establish intrinsic facts:

- `budget` is a positive scalar within the package limit;
- `method` is a supported value;
- candidate values are represented explicitly rather than inferred from
  vector length;
- local properties obey a cross-property rule.

It cannot establish that selected columns exist in a later dataset, that a
candidate count fits the number of available features, or that case weights
match the row count. Those requirements become checkable only when both the
specification and dataset are present.

`prepare()` is therefore not a second constructor that repeats validation. It
is a contextual operation that combines already-established intrinsic facts
with dataset facts and returns a stronger value. `PreparedRun` can carry the
resolved columns, normalized candidate plan, data fingerprint, and any
diagnostics or provenance needed by execution.

This is the temporal rule demonstrated particularly clearly by the public
design of rtemis: check **as early as possible, as late as necessary**.
Declaration errors whose inputs are already available can fail when a
property specification is created. Configuration errors can fail before an
expensive training run. Data-bound requirements—candidate counts relative to
features, selected names relative to columns, or weights relative to
rows—must wait until the data exists, but should run immediately then.
Deferral is not omission. The future requirement is declared early and
discharged at the first boundary with enough information.

The downstream payoff is observable. `execute()` no longer:

- rechecks scalar shape and local ranges;
- guesses whether a vector denotes one value or several candidates;
- repeatedly looks up or validates column names;
- discovers an impossible request after expensive work has begun.

The representation records that preparation occurred. If the dataset can
change, the contract must say whether `PreparedRun` owns a snapshot, records
an identity/version to check, or must be rebuilt. Construction cannot certify
an external resource forever.

## Supported transformations and cost

Property and class validators are hot-path code because supported property
replacement revalidates. Keep them pure and inexpensive. Multi-property
invariants require grouped replacement, such as `S7::set_props()`, so valid
transitions are not rejected at an invalid intermediate state.

Bulk operations may defer validation and validate the final value once, but
an unchecked path transfers the proof obligation to its caller. Such paths
are implementation techniques, not public evidence of validity.

Every exported transformation should state its postcondition:

- does it return another intrinsically valid `RunSpecification`?
- does changing a context-sensitive field invalidate preparation?
- does it preserve unknown foreign content?
- can reference-valued contents change behind the object's back?

Construction certificates remain useful only when their supported update
paths preserve the advertised meaning.

## Conditions, diagnostics, and outcomes

Conditions and values serve different control-flow contracts.

- Use classed conditions for contract violations, impossible requests, and
  failures that should unwind unless handled.
- Store diagnostics on unknown or partial parse variants when callers need
  to inspect and preserve them as data.
- Use an outcome family when success, rejection, cancellation, or failure is
  an expected result of a domain operation.

The conversion point should be explicit. A batch runner might catch selected
conditions around one task and produce a `TaskFailed` outcome, while
programmer errors continue to propagate. Chapter 5 defines the composition
policy for those outcomes; merely defining variant classes does not decide
whether failures short-circuit or accumulate.

The distinction is easiest to understand narratively. If a caller asks for a
negative budget, no lawful request exists: the boundary signals a classed
condition and unwinds. If a remote job was accepted but later timed out,
`TaskFailed` may be an ordinary result that a batch report must retain beside
completed tasks. A warning can describe a recoverable normalization, while a
diagnostic attached to `PartialSpecification` explains preserved uncertainty.
The same words—error, warning, failure—are not interchangeable channels.
Choose according to the control-flow promise callers need, then provide one
deliberate adapter where a selected condition becomes an outcome value.

For caller-facing conditions, `cli::cli_abort()` can provide structured,
classed errors while `rlang::caller_arg()` and `rlang::caller_env()` preserve
the user's argument name and call context. Validator messages should remain
short statements of violated laws.

## Make the retained knowledge testable

Tests should establish both rejection and simplification:

- unlawful known values fail at the boundary with useful diagnostics;
- tolerant parsing returns the correct known, unknown, or partial variant;
- compilation rejects variants unsupported by its target policy;
- supported updates preserve intrinsic invariants;
- preparation rejects contextually impossible requests before execution;
- execution accepts `PreparedRun` without repeating earlier checks;
- projections of an authoritative rule agree on representative and boundary
  cases.

Example tests establish named cases, but generated and property-based tests
exercise the laws across a much larger input space. Generate lawful
`RunSpecification` values and check that supported updates preserve validity;
generate loose inputs and check that parse/render normalization is
idempotent; generate model values and check round-trip equivalence under the
relation the API actually promises. Shrinking is especially valuable because
it reduces a failed law to a small counterexample rather than a large random
fixture.

The public s7contract package develops this direction explicitly: interfaces
name required generics, traits register implementations, and generative laws
test the behavioral part of a contract that a dispatch table cannot see.
Using that package is optional; writing executable laws is not. An interface
is never only a list of method names.

The central success criterion is not the number of validators. It is how much
less uncertainty downstream code must reconstruct. When the boundaries are
doing their jobs, a calm middle emerges: core functions accept domain values,
perform domain work, and return domain values. They do not contain a haze of
`is.character()` checks, repeated parsing, and defensive branches. Suspicion
is concentrated at the edges, where errors can be local and informative, and
the middle is free to express the actual computation.
